title: Dermatology
summary: How to read skin the way a clinician does: name the lesion, name the pattern, then decide whether it is a nuisance, an infection, a cancer, or an emergency. Covers rashes, infections, drug eruptions, skin cancer, wounds, and pediatric skin.

lessons.title: Skin structure and the language of lesions
lessons.body:
Skin is the largest organ in the body, roughly `1.5` to `2.0` square meters and about `15%` of body weight. It is a barrier, a thermostat, a sensor, and a vitamin D factory. Nearly every skin complaint makes sense once you know which layer is damaged.

## Three layers

The outer layer (epidermis) is dead-cell armor on top of live cells. It has no blood vessels of its own; it feeds by diffusion from below. Cells are born at the bottom (stratum basale), climb for about `28` days, and flake off the top (stratum corneum). Pigment cells (melanocytes) sit in that bottom layer and hand pigment packets to neighbors.

The middle layer (dermis) is the working floor: collagen, elastin, blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands, oil glands, hair follicles. Damage that reaches here bleeds and scars. Below that is fat (subcutis, or hypodermis), which insulates, cushions, and stores energy.

> **Key:** Damage confined to the epidermis heals without a scar. Once the injury crosses into the dermis, you get bleeding, pain, and scar tissue.

## Primary lesions

A primary lesion is the change the disease made first, before scratching or time altered it. Learn these nine cold, because every rash description starts here.

| Lesion | Definition |
|---|---|
| Macule | Flat color change, under `1 cm` |
| Patch | Flat color change, over `1 cm` |
| Papule | Raised solid bump, under `1 cm` |
| Plaque | Raised flat-topped area, over `1 cm` |
| Nodule | Solid bump deeper than a papule, over `1 cm` |
| Vesicle | Clear fluid blister, under `1 cm` |
| Bulla | Clear fluid blister, over `1 cm` |
| Pustule | Bump filled with pus |
| Wheal | Swollen pink hive, gone within `24` hours |

The recurring cutoff is `1 cm`. Flat versus raised, and fluid versus solid, does the rest of the sorting.

## Secondary lesions

Secondary lesions are what happens next. Scale is flaking of the dead outer layer. Crust is dried serum, blood, or pus (a scab). An erosion is loss of epidermis only, so it heals clean. An ulcer goes into the dermis or deeper, so it scars. Lichenification is leathery thickened skin with exaggerated lines from chronic rubbing. An excoriation is a linear scratch mark the patient made themselves.

> **On shift:** Excoriations tell you the rash itches even when the patient downplays it. Lichenification tells you it has itched for months.

## Bleeding into skin

When blood leaks out of vessels into the skin, it cannot be pushed away. Press a glass slide or your finger on the lesion (diascopy): red from dilated vessels blanches white; red from leaked blood does not.

Petechiae are pinpoint non-blanching spots under `2 mm`. Purpura are `2 mm` to `1 cm`. Ecchymosis is a bruise larger than `1 cm`. All three are non-blanching.

> **Trap:** A non-blanching rash is a different problem than a blanching one. Blanching means vessels are open and full. Non-blanching means blood is outside the vessels, which raises platelet problems, vasculitis, and meningococcal sepsis.
keyPoints: Epidermis has no blood supply and heals without scarring; dermis injury bleeds and scars.
The primary-lesion cutoff is 1 cm: macule/patch, papule/plaque, vesicle/bulla.
Secondary lesions are what time and scratching did: scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, lichenification, excoriation.
Petechiae under 2 mm, purpura 2 mm to 1 cm, ecchymosis over 1 cm, all non-blanching.
Blanching means blood inside vessels; non-blanching means blood has leaked out.

checks.q: A flat, brown, non-raised spot measuring 6 mm is best described as a:
checks.why: Flat and under 1 cm is a macule. A patch is flat but over 1 cm. Papule and plaque are raised.

checks.q: You press a glass slide over a red rash and the color does not fade. This tells you:
choices: Blood has leaked out of the vessels
checks.why: Non-blanching means extravasated blood (petechiae, purpura, ecchymosis). Dilated vessels blanch because you push the blood out. Hives blanch and resolve within 24 hours.

checks.q: A shallow lesion that has lost only the epidermis is an erosion. The key clinical consequence is that it:
checks.why: Erosion is epidermis-only, so it re-epithelializes without a scar. An ulcer reaches the dermis or deeper and does scar.

lessons.title: Reading a rash: distribution, configuration, and documentation
lessons.body:
Two skin diseases can share the exact same bump. What separates them is where the bumps are and how they are arranged. Experienced clinicians diagnose from across the room by pattern, then confirm by touching.

## Morphology first, always

Describe in a fixed order so nothing gets skipped: primary lesion, color, size, configuration, distribution, secondary change. A usable note reads like this: "Multiple `2` to `4 mm` erythematous papules with fine scale, grouped in annular plaques, on bilateral antecubital fossae, with excoriations." That sentence contains the diagnosis even if you never name it.

> **Key:** Name the lesion before you name the disease. If you jump to a disease name, you will fit the findings to your guess instead of the other way around.

## Distribution: where it lives

- Flexural means the soft creases: inner elbows, behind the knees, neck. Classic for eczema (atopic dermatitis) in children and adults.
- Extensor means the outer surfaces: elbows, knees, shins. Classic for psoriasis.
- Dermatomal means a single stripe on one side that stops sharply at the midline, following one spinal nerve's territory. That is shingles (herpes zoster) until proven otherwise.
- Acral means hands, feet, and face edges. Sun-exposed means face, ears, dorsal forearms, upper back, and the bald scalp.
- Intertriginous means skin-on-skin folds: groin, under breasts, abdominal folds, between toes. Warm and damp, so think yeast and fungus.

## Configuration: how lesions relate to each other

- Annular is ring-shaped with a clear center. Ringworm (tinea corporis) is the prototype.
- Target lesions have three zones, a dark or blistered center, a pale ring, and a red outer ring. That is erythema multiforme.
- Grouped vesicles on a red base (herpetiform) means a herpes family virus.
- Linear means something touched the skin in a line: poison ivy, a scratch.
- Koebnerization is new lesions appearing exactly along a scratch or scar. Psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo do this.

> **On the exam:** Dermatomal plus painful plus vesicles equals zoster. Annular plus scaly edge plus central clearing equals tinea. Target lesions equal erythema multiforme. Those three patterns carry a lot of questions.

## Skin tone matters

Fitzpatrick types run `I` (always burns, never tans) through `VI` (never burns, deeply pigmented). Redness (erythema) is harder to see in types `IV` to `VI` and may look violet, gray, or simply darker than surrounding skin. Use touch and comparison: warmth, swelling, and induration do not depend on color. Cyanosis and pallor are checked at mucous membranes, palms, and nail beds.

## Two bedside maneuvers

Diascopy is the glass-slide press that separates blanching from non-blanching.

Nikolsky sign is positive when firm lateral pressure on normal-looking skin next to a blister makes the top layer slide or shear off. A positive Nikolsky means the epidermis is detaching in sheets, which points to Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, staph scalded skin, or pemphigus vulgaris. It is never a benign finding.

## When to biopsy

Biopsy when a lesion might be cancer, when a rash is not responding to reasonable treatment, when a blistering or vasculitic disease is suspected, or when the diagnosis changes management substantially. Pigmented lesions concerning for melanoma get a full-thickness excisional biopsy when feasible, because depth determines staging and a shave cut can transect the tumor.
keyPoints: Describe morphology, configuration, and distribution before naming a disease.
Flexural suggests eczema, extensor suggests psoriasis, dermatomal suggests zoster.
Annular with scaly border equals tinea; target lesions equal erythema multiforme; grouped vesicles equal herpes family.
A positive Nikolsky sign (skin shears with lateral pressure) means SJS/TEN, staph scalded skin, or pemphigus.
Suspected melanoma gets a full-thickness excisional biopsy because Breslow depth drives staging.

checks.q: A 63-year-old has grouped painful vesicles in a band on the left flank that stops abruptly at the midline. This distribution is called:
checks.why: A unilateral stripe respecting the midline follows one dermatome, which means herpes zoster. Flexural is creases, intertriginous is skin folds, acral is hands and feet.

checks.q: Lateral pressure on normal skin beside a blister causes the top layer to slide off. This finding:
choices: Is a normal variant in older adults
Indicates the epidermis is separating and suggests SJS/TEN or staph scalded skin
checks.why: That is a positive Nikolsky sign, a marker of epidermal detachment. It is seen in SJS/TEN, staph scalded skin syndrome, and pemphigus vulgaris, and is never normal.

checks.q: Why is an excisional (full-thickness) biopsy preferred for a lesion suspicious for melanoma?
choices: It is faster than a shave biopsy
It preserves depth so Breslow thickness can be measured
checks.why: Breslow depth drives staging and prognosis. A shave biopsy can cut through the base of the tumor and make depth unmeasurable. Cosmetics and speed are not the deciding factor.

lessons.title: Bacterial skin infections and the one that kills
lessons.body:
Almost all skin infections come from two bugs: *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Streptococcus pyogenes* (group A strep). What changes is how deep they got.

## Surface: impetigo

Impetigo lives in the epidermis only. Classic non-bullous impetigo makes crusted erosions with a thick honey-colored crust, usually around the nose and mouth in children aged `2` to `5`. Bullous impetigo, caused by a staph toxin, makes flaccid blisters that rupture into shallow round erosions with a collarette of scale.

Treatment is topical mupirocin `2%` three times daily for `5` days if limited, or oral cephalexin or doxycycline if widespread. It is contagious by direct contact; children can usually return to school `24` hours after starting treatment.

## Follicles: folliculitis to carbuncle

Folliculitis is a pustule centered on a hair. Hot-tub folliculitis from *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* appears `1` to `3` days after a poorly chlorinated tub and usually self-resolves. A furuncle (boil) is one infected follicle that walled off into an abscess. A carbuncle is several adjacent furuncles draining through multiple openings, and it is more likely to come with fever.

## Abscess: cut it

An abscess is a pocket of pus in the dermis or below: fluctuant, tender, warm, often with a point. Antibiotics alone do not fix it, because the drug does not penetrate pus.

> **Key:** The treatment for an abscess is incision and drainage. Antibiotics are an add-on, not a substitute.

Add oral antibiotics after drainage when there is surrounding cellulitis, fever or other systemic signs, immunosuppression, extremes of age, an abscess larger than about `2 cm`, or facial and hand locations. Bedside ultrasound separates an abscess (a dark fluid pocket) from cellulitis alone.

## Deeper: cellulitis and erysipelas

Cellulitis is infection of the dermis and subcutaneous fat: warm, red, swollen, tender, with indistinct borders that fade into normal skin. Usually staph or strep, often starting from a crack such as tinea pedis between the toes.

Erysipelas is shallower, in the upper dermis and lymphatics, almost always group A strep. It is fire-engine red with a sharply raised border you can feel with your eyes closed, and it comes with abrupt fever and chills.

> **Trap:** Bilateral lower-leg redness is rarely bilateral cellulitis. It is far more often stasis dermatitis from venous insufficiency, which is itchy rather than exquisitely tender and is usually afebrile.

MRSA is the concern with purulent infections, abscesses, recent hospitalization, or recent antibiotics. Oral MRSA coverage is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, or clindamycin. Non-purulent cellulitis is treated for strep with cephalexin `500 mg` four times daily. Always mark the border of redness with a pen and the time so progression is objective.

## The emergency: necrotizing fasciitis

This is infection racing along the fascial plane, destroying tissue faster than antibiotics can travel. The earliest and most reliable sign is pain out of proportion to the skin findings, because nerves are being destroyed before the surface looks bad.

Later signs: rapid progression over hours, skin that turns dusky or purple, hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus (crackling from gas), anesthesia over the area, and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score bundles lab values such as C-reactive protein, white count, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose into a risk number, but a low score never rules it out.

> **On shift:** Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical diagnosis. Broad antibiotics, fluids, and an immediate surgical consult for operative debridement. Mortality runs roughly `20%` to `30%` and rises with every hour of delay. Imaging must not delay the operating room.
keyPoints: Honey-colored crust equals impetigo; treat topically with mupirocin if limited.
Abscess treatment is incision and drainage; antibiotics are adjunctive.
Cellulitis has indistinct borders; erysipelas is sharply demarcated, raised, and strep.
Purulent infection means cover MRSA with TMP-SMX, doxycycline, or clindamycin.
Pain out of proportion, crepitus, or dusky skin means necrotizing fasciitis and immediate surgery.

checks.q: A 34-year-old has a 3 cm fluctuant, tender thigh mass with surrounding redness and a temperature of 38.3 C. The most important next step is:
choices: Incision and drainage, then oral antibiotics covering MRSA
Warm compresses and recheck in one week
checks.why: Fluctuance means pus, and pus must be drained; antibiotics do not penetrate an abscess. Fever, size over 2 cm, and surrounding cellulitis justify adding oral MRSA coverage after drainage.

checks.q: Which finding most strongly suggests necrotizing fasciitis rather than uncomplicated cellulitis?
choices: Pain far out of proportion to the visible skin findings
checks.why: Pain out of proportion is the earliest reliable clue because the infection destroys nerves along the fascia before the surface looks severe. A sharp raised border is erysipelas, honey crust is impetigo, bilateral itching is stasis dermatitis.

checks.q: Compared with cellulitis, erysipelas characteristically has:
choices: A sharply demarcated, raised border with abrupt fever
checks.why: Erysipelas involves the superficial dermis and lymphatics, producing a palpable sharp edge and sudden systemic symptoms. Cellulitis is deeper with borders that fade gradually into normal skin.

lessons.title: Viral skin disease from herpes to measles
lessons.body:
Viruses either sit in nerves and come back (herpes family), hijack skin cells to grow (warts, molluscum), or paint the whole body during a systemic illness (measles, fifth disease, roseola).

## Herpes simplex

HSV-1 classically causes oral lesions and HSV-2 genital, but either virus can live in either site. First infection is the worst: painful grouped vesicles on a red base, fever, and swollen nodes lasting `10` to `14` days. The virus then hides in the nerve root ganglion for life and reactivates with stress, illness, sunlight, or menses, usually with a tingling warning (prodrome) hours before lesions appear.

Treat with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir. Antivirals shorten the episode by roughly a day and work best started at the prodrome. Valacyclovir `2 g` twice in one day is a common cold-sore regimen; genital first episodes usually get `7` to `10` days of therapy.

Two complications matter. Herpetic whitlow is HSV in a fingertip, common in health workers and thumb-sucking children, and it is not an abscess: do not incise it. Eczema herpeticum is HSV spreading across eczematous skin as monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever; it is an emergency needing systemic acyclovir.

> **Trap:** A painful, swollen fingertip with clustered vesicles is herpetic whitlow, not a felon. Incision risks spreading the virus and does not help.

## Varicella and zoster

Chickenpox (varicella) gives crops of lesions in all stages at once, macules to papules to vesicles to crusts, spreading from trunk outward, including the scalp and mouth. Patients are contagious from about `48` hours before the rash until every lesion crusts.

The same virus retreats into a sensory ganglion and returns decades later as shingles (herpes zoster): burning pain for `2` to `3` days, then grouped vesicles in one dermatome, one side, not crossing the midline. Antivirals help most when started within `72` hours of rash onset; they cut acute pain and reduce postherpetic neuralgia, the nerve pain that persists after the rash heals.

Two special sites. Zoster ophthalmicus involves the first division of the trigeminal nerve; vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) predict eye involvement and require same-day ophthalmology. Ramsay Hunt syndrome is zoster of the facial nerve: vesicles in the ear canal plus one-sided facial droop, sometimes with hearing loss and vertigo.

> **Key:** The antiviral window for zoster is `72` hours from rash onset. After that the benefit falls sharply, though it is still offered for new lesions or eye involvement.

## Growths

Warts come from human papillomavirus. Common warts are rough papules with black dots (thrombosed capillaries); plantar warts grow inward and interrupt skin lines; flat warts are small and numerous. Most resolve on their own in `1` to `2` years; treatment is salicylic acid or cryotherapy.

Molluscum contagiosum makes dome-shaped pearly papules with a central dimple (umbilication), spread by contact and self-inoculation, and resolves over months.

## Systemic viral rashes

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackievirus A16) gives painful oral ulcers plus oval gray vesicles on palms, soles, and buttocks in children under `5`.

Measles follows the three C's: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, plus high fever. Koplik spots, tiny white grains on a red buccal membrane, appear `1` to `2` days before the rash. The rash starts at the hairline and moves down, becoming confluent. It is extremely contagious by airborne spread, so mask and isolate immediately.

Fifth disease (parvovirus B19) gives slapped-cheek redness then a lacy rash on the arms; the child is no longer contagious once the rash appears. Roseola (HHV-6) gives `3` days of high fever that breaks, then a pink trunk rash appears as the child improves.
keyPoints: Grouped vesicles on a red base equals a herpes family virus.
Zoster antivirals work best within 72 hours of rash onset.
Vesicles on the nose tip (Hutchinson sign) predict eye involvement and need same-day ophthalmology.
Herpetic whitlow is not drained; eczema herpeticum needs systemic acyclovir.
Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis plus Koplik spots means measles: airborne isolation now.

checks.q: A 68-year-old reports 2 days of burning right chest pain, now with grouped vesicles in one band that stops at the midline. Rash began 24 hours ago. Best management includes:
choices: Start oral antiviral therapy now, since it is within the 72-hour window
checks.why: This is herpes zoster, and antivirals started within 72 hours of rash onset shorten the episode and reduce postherpetic neuralgia. Antibacterials and drainage do nothing for a viral dermatomal eruption.

checks.q: Tiny white grains on a red buccal mucosa appearing one to two days before a descending rash are:
checks.why: Koplik spots are the pathognomonic early sign of measles. Thrush is a removable white plaque from Candida, aphthous ulcers are painful punched-out sores, and molluscum is a skin papule, not a mucosal finding.

checks.q: A child with known atopic dermatitis develops fever and hundreds of uniform punched-out erosions across the eczematous areas. This is:
checks.why: Monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczematous skin with fever is eczema herpeticum, a disseminated HSV emergency needing systemic acyclovir. Topical therapy is inadequate and molluscum is painless and afebrile.

lessons.title: Fungal infections and skin infestations
lessons.body:
Fungi like warm, damp, dark places. Parasites like people. Both make itchy rashes, and both are diagnosed with cheap bedside tests instead of guessing.

## Dermatophytes: the tineas

Dermatophytes eat keratin, so they live in the dead outer layer, hair, and nails. They are named by location, not by organism.

- Tinea corporis (ringworm) on the body: an annular plaque with a scaly, raised, advancing edge and a clearing center. There is no worm.
- Tinea cruris (jock itch) in the groin: spares the scrotum, which distinguishes it from candida.
- Tinea pedis (athlete's foot): scaling and maceration between the fourth and fifth toes, or a dry moccasin pattern over the sole. It is the usual entry wound for lower-leg cellulitis.
- Tinea capitis on the scalp: scaly patches with broken-off hairs and black dots, often with swollen neck nodes. This one needs oral therapy, usually griseofulvin for `6` to `8` weeks or terbinafine for `2` to `6` weeks, because topicals cannot reach the hair shaft.
- Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) in the nails: thick, yellow, crumbling nails. Oral terbinafine `250 mg` daily for `6` weeks for fingernails and `12` weeks for toenails.

> **Key:** Skin and groin tinea respond to topical antifungals. Hair and nails require oral therapy because the drug must grow out with the keratin.

Tinea versicolor is different: it comes from a yeast, *Malassezia*, that everyone carries. It makes fine scaly patches on the chest, back, and shoulders that fail to tan, so they look light on tan skin and slightly darker on pale skin. Treat with topical selenium sulfide or ketoconazole; pigment takes months to even out.

## The KOH prep

Scrape scale from the advancing edge onto a slide, add potassium hydroxide, and warm it. KOH dissolves human cells and leaves fungal walls, so you see branching filaments (hyphae) in dermatophytes or the short hyphae plus spores of versicolor, described as spaghetti and meatballs.

> **Trap:** Putting a topical steroid on tinea calms the redness and itch but lets the fungus spread with a strange, poorly defined border. That is called tinea incognito. Confirm with KOH before reaching for steroids.

## Candida

*Candida albicans* is a yeast that prefers moist folds. Candidal intertrigo is a beefy-red, sharply bordered plaque in the groin, under breasts, or in abdominal folds, with small pustules just outside the main patch (satellite lesions) that give it away. Risk goes up with diabetes, obesity, antibiotics, and incontinence. Treat with a topical azole such as clotrimazole plus aggressive drying.

Oral thrush is white curd-like plaques that scrape off leaving a raw red base, treated with nystatin swish-and-swallow or oral fluconazole. Thrush in an adult with no obvious cause should prompt thought about inhaled steroids, diabetes, or immunosuppression including HIV.

## Scabies

A mite burrows into the outer skin layer and lays eggs. The itch is an allergic reaction, so it starts `2` to `6` weeks after a first infestation but within days on reinfestation. It is worst at night and out of proportion to what you see.

Look for thin wavy burrows in finger webs, wrists, waistline, axillae, and genitals. Infants can have involvement of the palms, soles, and scalp. Treat with permethrin `5%` cream applied neck-down and left on `8` to `14` hours, repeated in `7` days, plus oral ivermectin in resistant or crusted cases.

> **On shift:** Treat all household members and close contacts at the same time even if they have no itch, and wash bedding and clothing in hot water or bag them for `72` hours. Skipping contacts is why scabies comes back. Itching can persist `2` to `4` weeks after successful treatment and is not treatment failure.

## Lice and bed bugs

Head lice are diagnosed by finding nits cemented to hair shafts within `1 cm` of the scalp; treat with permethrin `1%` and comb. Body lice live in clothing seams, not on the body, so the clothing is treated. Pubic lice suggest checking for other sexually transmitted infections. Bed bugs bite exposed skin in a line of three, feed at night, and live in mattress seams, so treatment is the environment, not the patient.
keyPoints: Tinea of hair and nails needs oral antifungals; skin and groin tinea respond to topicals.
KOH prep from the advancing scaly edge shows hyphae and confirms dermatophyte infection.
Candidal intertrigo is beefy red with satellite pustules; tinea cruris spares the scrotum.
Scabies: night itch, web-space burrows, permethrin 5% repeated in 7 days, treat all contacts.
Steroids on tinea cause tinea incognito, spreading fungus with a blurred border.

checks.q: A 7-year-old has scaly scalp patches with broken hairs and tender occipital nodes. Correct treatment is:
choices: Oral griseofulvin for 6 to 8 weeks, or terbinafine for 2 to 6 weeks
checks.why: Tinea capitis involves the hair shaft, which topicals cannot penetrate, so oral antifungal therapy is required. Shampoo only reduces spore shedding, steroids worsen fungal infection, and permethrin treats scabies and lice.

checks.q: A beefy-red plaque under the breast with small pustules just beyond its edge most suggests:
checks.why: Satellite pustules outside a sharply bordered red plaque in a moist fold are classic for Candida. Tinea clears centrally with a scaly advancing edge, and erysipelas is febrile and acutely tender.

checks.q: After correct permethrin treatment for scabies, a patient still itches at 2 weeks. The best explanation is:
choices: Treatment failure requiring immediate retreatment with ivermectin
Normal post-scabetic itch from persistent allergic reaction, which can last 2 to 4 weeks
checks.why: The itch is an immune reaction to mite antigen and outlasts the dead mites by weeks. New burrows or new lesions, not itch alone, indicate failure.

lessons.title: Itchy and scaly: the inflammatory rashes
lessons.body:
This group is not infection. It is the immune system reacting, either to something it touched, something it inherited, or nothing identifiable at all.

## Atopic dermatitis (eczema)

A leaky skin barrier, often from a filaggrin protein defect, lets water out and irritants in. The result is dry, itchy skin that inflames when scratched. It travels with asthma and hay fever as the atopic triad.

Distribution changes with age: cheeks and outer arms in infants, flexural creases (inner elbows, behind the knees) in children and adults. Chronic disease adds lichenification.

Management starts with the barrier: thick emollient ointments at least twice daily, lukewarm short baths, and moisturizer applied within `3` minutes of patting dry. Flares get topical steroids, and severe disease gets calcineurin inhibitors or biologics such as dupilumab.

> **Key:** Eczema is the itch that rashes, not the rash that itches. Breaking the scratch cycle is most of the treatment.

## Contact dermatitis

Irritant contact dermatitis is chemical damage, not allergy. It burns and stings, appears in anyone with enough exposure, and shows up within minutes to hours. Frequent hand washing is the classic cause, and it accounts for roughly `80%` of contact dermatitis.

Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed T-cell reaction that requires prior sensitization, peaks `48` to `72` hours after exposure, and itches rather than burns. Poison ivy leaves linear streaks of vesicles; nickel from jewelry and belt buckles makes a rash in the shape of the object. Patch testing identifies the culprit. Severe or widespread cases get oral prednisone tapered over `14` to `21` days, because a short `5`-day burst often lets it rebound.

## Psoriasis

Keratinocytes turn over in `3` to `5` days instead of `28`, so scale piles up faster than it sheds. Plaques are well-demarcated, salmon-red, with thick silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp, and the gluteal cleft. Scraping the scale off exposes pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign). Nails show pitting, oil spots, and separation from the bed (onycholysis).

About `30%` of patients develop psoriatic arthritis, often with sausage-shaped digits (dactylitis) and distal finger joint involvement. Psoriasis also carries a higher rate of metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease, so it is a systemic disease, not a cosmetic one.

## Seborrheic dermatitis

Greasy yellow scale on the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and central chest, driven by *Malassezia* yeast in oily areas. Treat with ketoconazole shampoo or low-potency steroid. Sudden severe seborrheic dermatitis in a young adult should prompt HIV testing.

## Lichen planus and pityriasis rosea

Lichen planus is remembered by the six P's: purple, polygonal, pruritic, planar (flat-topped) papules with fine white lines (Wickham striae), usually on the wrists and ankles, often with lacy white oral patches. It is associated with hepatitis C.

Pityriasis rosea starts with a single large scaly oval (the herald patch), then a week or two later a shower of smaller ovals along skin lines on the trunk in a Christmas-tree pattern. It resolves in `6` to `8` weeks without treatment.

> **Trap:** Secondary syphilis mimics pityriasis rosea but involves the palms and soles. Any papulosquamous rash on the palms and soles gets syphilis serology.

## Hives and angioedema

Urticaria is mast-cell histamine release making wheals that individually last under `24` hours and blanch. Acute urticaria is under `6` weeks, usually from infection, food, or drugs. Chronic urticaria is `6` weeks or more and is most often idiopathic. First-line treatment is a second-generation antihistamine such as cetirizine, dosed up to four times the standard amount if needed.

Angioedema is deeper swelling of lips, tongue, and eyelids, tight rather than itchy. Histamine-driven angioedema comes with hives; bradykinin-driven angioedema from ACE inhibitors or hereditary C1 inhibitor deficiency has no hives and does not respond to antihistamines, steroids, or epinephrine. Airway is the priority either way.

## The steroid ladder

Potency runs class `1` (super-high, clobetasol `0.05%`) to class `7` (low, hydrocortisone `1%` or `2.5%`). Use low potency on the face, groin, and folds, where thin skin absorbs more and thins further. Use higher potency on palms, soles, and thick plaques. Ointments beat creams for potency and dryness; creams are better in moist folds. Limit potent steroids to about `2` weeks continuously to avoid skin thinning (atrophy), stretch marks, and visible vessels.
keyPoints: Eczema is flexural, dry, and intensely itchy; emollients are the foundation of therapy.
Allergic contact dermatitis peaks 48 to 72 hours later and itches; irritant burns and needs no sensitization.
Psoriasis: extensor silvery plaques, Auspitz sign, nail pitting, 30% get psoriatic arthritis.
A papulosquamous rash involving palms and soles means test for secondary syphilis.
ACE-inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated: no hives, and antihistamines and epinephrine do not fix it.

checks.q: A 28-year-old develops an itchy rash in linear streaks of vesicles on the forearm two days after yard work. The mechanism is:
choices: Direct chemical irritation with no immune memory
checks.why: Poison ivy is allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed type IV T-cell reaction peaking 48 to 72 hours after exposure. IgE reactions occur within minutes, and irritant dermatitis burns immediately without sensitization.

checks.q: Scraping the silvery scale off a well-demarcated elbow plaque produces pinpoint bleeding. This sign and diagnosis are:
checks.why: Auspitz sign reflects the dilated capillaries just under a thinned suprapapillary plate in psoriasis. Nikolsky is epidermal shearing, and Wickham striae are white lines on lichen planus papules.

checks.q: A patient on lisinopril has lip and tongue swelling with no hives and no itch. The most important understanding is:
choices: Antihistamines and steroids will reverse it promptly
It is bradykinin-mediated, so antihistamines, steroids, and epinephrine are largely ineffective and airway is the priority
It should be treated with topical steroid
checks.why: ACE inhibitor angioedema comes from bradykinin accumulation, not histamine, so standard allergy drugs do not work. Airway monitoring and stopping the drug are the key actions.

lessons.title: Drug eruptions and the skin emergencies
lessons.body:
Most drug rashes are annoying. A few peel the patient. The job is telling them apart within minutes, because the first action in every severe one is the same: stop the drug.

## The common one: morbilliform drug rash

Small pink-red macules and papules that start on the trunk and spread outward, becoming confluent, usually `4` to `14` days after a new drug starts. The patient itches but is otherwise well, with no mucous membrane involvement, no blisters, and no fever. Common culprits are penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides, allopurinol, and anticonvulsants. Stop the drug and treat with antihistamines and topical steroids.

> **Key:** Mucous membranes, blisters, skin pain, and fever are the four features that turn a simple drug rash into an emergency.

## Fixed drug eruption

One or a few round, dusky violet plaques that recur in exactly the same spot every time the drug is taken, often on the lips, genitals, or hands, and leaving gray-brown pigment behind. NSAIDs, sulfonamides, and tetracyclines are typical. The repeat-same-site pattern is the diagnosis.

## Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis

These are one disease separated by how much skin detaches:

- SJS: under `10%` of body surface area
- SJS/TEN overlap: `10%` to `30%`
- TEN: over `30%`

Onset is typically `1` to `3` weeks after the drug. A flu-like prodrome and painful skin come first, then dusky red macules with detachment, a positive Nikolsky sign, and erosions at two or more mucosal sites: eyes, mouth, genitals. Skin pain before visible rash is a red flag.

Usual offenders are allopurinol, sulfonamides, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin, nevirapine, and NSAIDs of the oxicam class. Mortality is roughly `5%` for SJS and `30%` or more for TEN, tracked by the SCORTEN score.

Management: stop the drug immediately, transfer to a burn unit, and treat like a burn with fluid resuscitation, temperature control, wound care, and early ophthalmology involvement to prevent blindness. Steroids remain controversial; prophylactic antibiotics are not given.

## DRESS

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is slower: `2` to `8` weeks after the drug starts. It brings a widespread rash, facial swelling, fever, large lymph nodes, eosinophilia often above `700` cells per microliter, and organ injury, most often hepatitis. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin, and minocycline are typical. Stop the drug and start systemic steroids, often tapered over weeks because DRESS relapses. Thyroid function must be rechecked months later since late thyroiditis is common.

> **Trap:** DRESS is missed because the timing is too long for people to connect it to a drug started two months ago. Any new rash plus fever plus eosinophilia plus abnormal liver enzymes should make you review the full medication list back `8` weeks.

## Erythema multiforme

Target lesions with three zones, favoring the hands, forearms, and feet, symmetric and acral. The main cause is infection, especially HSV, not drugs. EM minor has little or no mucosal involvement; EM major has mucosal lesions. It is a distinct disease from SJS, which is drug-driven and centrally distributed with true skin detachment.

## Anaphylaxis

Rapid multi-system allergic reaction: skin (hives, flushing, swelling) plus respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal involvement. The first and only lifesaving drug is epinephrine `0.3 mg` intramuscularly into the outer thigh (`0.15 mg` for children under `30 kg`), repeatable every `5` to `15` minutes. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts and never delay epinephrine. Observe for a biphasic reaction that can occur `4` to `12` hours later.

## Two more that peel or bleed

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome affects children under `5` and comes from a staph toxin that splits the epidermis. It gives fever, red tender skin, and peeling with a positive Nikolsky, but mucous membranes are spared, which is the discriminator from TEN. Treat with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

Purpura fulminans and meningococcemia present as rapidly spreading non-blanching purpura with fever, hypotension, and shock. This is sepsis with disseminated clotting. Blood cultures and immediate IV antibiotics, ideally within `1` hour, plus aggressive fluids.

> **On shift:** A febrile patient with a non-blanching rash gets treated as meningococcemia until proven otherwise. Do not wait for the rash to declare itself.
keyPoints: Morbilliform drug rash: 4 to 14 days out, itchy, well patient, no mucosal involvement.
SJS under 10% BSA, overlap 10 to 30%, TEN over 30%; both need burn unit care and the drug stopped.
DRESS appears 2 to 8 weeks out with fever, facial swelling, eosinophilia, and hepatitis.
Erythema multiforme is target lesions, acral, usually triggered by HSV, not drugs.
Anaphylaxis gets epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the thigh first; antihistamines never come first.

checks.q: A patient started allopurinol 5 weeks ago and now has a diffuse rash, facial swelling, temperature 38.8 C, eosinophils 1,400/microliter, and ALT three times normal. The diagnosis is:
checks.why: Delayed onset plus fever, facial edema, eosinophilia, and hepatitis defines DRESS. A simple morbilliform rash has no fever or organ injury, TEN features skin detachment and mucosal erosions, and EM shows target lesions.

checks.q: A child has fever, diffuse red tender skin that peels, and a positive Nikolsky sign, but the mouth, eyes, and genitals are normal. This points to:
checks.why: Mucosal sparing separates staph scalded skin from SJS/TEN, which require erosions at two or more mucosal sites. SSSS is toxin-mediated and treated with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

checks.q: An adult develops hives, wheezing, and a blood pressure of 82/50 minutes after a bee sting. The first action is:
choices: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM into the outer thigh
checks.why: Epinephrine IM is the only intervention that reverses anaphylaxis and must come first. Antihistamines, steroids, and bronchodilators are adjuncts and must never delay it.

lessons.title: Acne, rosacea, hair and nails
lessons.body:
These are the visits that fill a dermatology clinic. They are rarely dangerous and often deeply distressing, and the treatment ladders are testable.

## Acne vulgaris

Four things have to happen. The follicle opening plugs with sticky keratin, oil glands overproduce sebum under androgen stimulation, *Cutibacterium acnes* bacteria multiply in that oil, and inflammation follows.

Lesions map onto the steps. Closed comedones (whiteheads) and open comedones (blackheads, dark from oxidized keratin, not dirt) are the plug. Papules and pustules are inflammation. Nodules and cysts are deep inflammation that scars.

The ladder:

1. Comedonal acne: topical retinoid (tretinoin, adapalene) at night. Retinoids normalize keratin shedding and are the only agents that treat and prevent comedones.
2. Mild inflammatory acne: add benzoyl peroxide, which kills bacteria without creating resistance.
3. Moderate: add a topical antibiotic such as clindamycin, always paired with benzoyl peroxide to prevent resistance. Never use a topical antibiotic alone.
4. Moderate to severe: oral doxycycline `100 mg` daily for `3` months maximum, or hormonal therapy with combined oral contraceptives or spironolactone in women.
5. Severe nodulocystic or scarring acne: isotretinoin, usually `0.5` to `1.0 mg/kg/day` for a cumulative `120` to `150 mg/kg`.

> **Key:** Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen. In the United States it requires iPLEDGE enrollment, two forms of contraception, and monthly pregnancy tests for anyone who can become pregnant. Monitor lipids and liver enzymes.

## Hidradenitis suppurativa

Recurrent painful deep nodules, abscesses, and draining sinus tracts in the armpits, groin, and under the breasts, ending in rope-like scars. It is follicular occlusion, not poor hygiene, and it is strongly associated with smoking and obesity. Treatment runs from topical clindamycin and oral tetracyclines through adalimumab to surgery. Hurley stage `I` is isolated nodules, `II` is recurrent abscesses with tracts, `III` is diffuse involvement.

## Rosacea

Adults over `30`, often fair-skinned, with central facial redness. Subtypes: erythematotelangiectatic (flushing plus visible vessels), papulopustular (bumps and pustules with no comedones), phymatous (thickened nose, rhinophyma), and ocular (gritty, dry, red eyes, present in up to half of patients).

> **Trap:** Rosacea has no comedones. Blackheads mean acne, not rosacea. Topical steroids make rosacea worse and can cause steroid-induced rosacea.

Avoid triggers such as sun, heat, alcohol, and spicy food. Treat with topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin; papulopustular disease may need oral doxycycline. Laser treats the vessels.

## Hair loss

Alopecia areata is autoimmune: sudden smooth round bald patches with no scale or scarring, sometimes with exclamation-point hairs and nail pitting. It is associated with thyroid disease and vitiligo. Most single patches regrow within a year; treat with intralesional steroids.

Androgenetic alopecia is gradual and patterned, with a receding hairline and vertex thinning in men and widened part with preserved hairline in women. Treat with topical minoxidil, and finasteride `1 mg` in men.

Telogen effluvium is diffuse shedding that starts `2` to `3` months after a stressor: childbirth, surgery, severe illness, rapid weight loss, or a new medication. Hair follicles shift together into the resting phase. It self-resolves in `6` to `9` months once the trigger is removed.

Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia loses the follicle openings entirely and is permanent, so it needs prompt referral and biopsy.

## Nails

Onychomycosis is thick, yellow, crumbling nail. Confirm with KOH, PAS stain, or culture before committing someone to months of oral terbinafine, because up to half of thick nails are not fungal.

Acute paronychia is a painful red swelling of the nail fold, usually staph, treated with warm soaks and drainage if pus has collected. Chronic paronychia comes from repeated water exposure and is largely Candida and irritation.

An ingrown toenail (onychocryptosis) happens when the nail edge pierces the fold, usually from cutting the nail curved instead of straight across or from tight shoes. Treatment is partial nail avulsion; recurrent cases get the nail matrix destroyed chemically with phenol.

> **On shift:** A dark streak in a single nail that widens or spreads pigment onto the surrounding skin fold (Hutchinson sign of the nail) is melanoma until a biopsy says otherwise.
keyPoints: Topical retinoids are the backbone of acne and the only agent preventing comedones.
Never use a topical antibiotic for acne without benzoyl peroxide, to avoid resistance.
Isotretinoin requires iPLEDGE, two contraceptive methods, and monthly pregnancy testing.
Rosacea has no comedones and gets worse with topical steroids.
Telogen effluvium begins 2 to 3 months after a stressor and resolves in 6 to 9 months.

checks.q: A 17-year-old has scattered blackheads and whiteheads on the forehead with no inflammatory lesions. First-line therapy is:
choices: A topical retinoid such as adapalene
checks.why: Comedonal acne is a keratin plugging problem, and retinoids normalize shedding to treat and prevent comedones. Oral antibiotics are for inflammatory disease, isotretinoin is for severe scarring acne, and clindamycin alone breeds resistance.

checks.q: A 45-year-old has central facial flushing, telangiectasias, and pustules, but no comedones. She has been using a potent topical steroid, which worsened it. The diagnosis is:
checks.why: Absence of comedones plus flushing and telangiectasias defines rosacea, and potent topical steroids reliably worsen it. Acne requires comedones, and seborrheic dermatitis shows greasy scale rather than pustules with flushing.

checks.q: A woman reports heavy diffuse hair shedding beginning about 3 months after a major surgery. The scalp looks normal with no bald patches. This is:
checks.why: A stressor shifting follicles synchronously into resting phase causes diffuse shedding 2 to 3 months later, resolving in 6 to 9 months. Alopecia areata makes discrete smooth patches, and scarring alopecia loses follicular openings.

lessons.title: Skin cancer and the damage the sun leaves
lessons.body:
Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the United States, with more than `5` million cases treated each year. Almost all of it traces back to ultraviolet light breaking DNA in skin cells.

## Actinic keratosis: the warning

Actinic keratoses are rough, gritty, sandpaper-like pink patches on sun-exposed skin, often easier to feel than to see. They are precancerous: roughly `0.1%` to `1%` per lesion per year progress to squamous cell carcinoma, but a patient with dozens has meaningful cumulative risk.

Treat individual lesions with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy, or treat a whole field with topical `5`-fluorouracil, imiquimod, or photodynamic therapy. A lesion that is thick, tender, or bleeding is no longer just an actinic keratosis; biopsy it.

## Basal cell carcinoma

The most common cancer in humans, about `80%` of skin cancers. It arises in the deepest epidermal layer and grows slowly. The classic look is a pearly or translucent papule with rolled borders, fine surface vessels (telangiectasias), and a central ulcer that scabs, bleeds, heals, and comes back in the same place.

It metastasizes almost never, under `0.1%`, but it destroys locally, which is why a basal cell carcinoma near the eye, nose, or ear is a real problem. Treatment is excision, or Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk sites where tissue must be spared.

> **Key:** A sore on the face that keeps bleeding, healing, and returning over months is basal cell carcinoma until a biopsy proves otherwise.

## Squamous cell carcinoma

About `20%` of skin cancers. A firm, scaly, crusted red nodule or plaque, often tender, that may ulcerate. It favors the lip, ear, dorsal hands, and scalp. It can metastasize, roughly `2%` to `5%` overall but higher on the lip and ear and much higher in transplant patients on immunosuppression, whose squamous cell risk runs `65` to `100` times the general population.

A chronic wound or burn scar that becomes a growing ulcer is a Marjolin ulcer, a squamous cell carcinoma arising in scar tissue.

## Melanoma

Only about `1%` of skin cancers but the majority of skin cancer deaths, because it spreads early. Use ABCDE:

- **A**symmetry: one half does not match the other
- **B**order irregularity: notched, scalloped, poorly defined
- **C**olor variation: multiple shades of brown, black, red, white, or blue in one lesion
- **D**iameter over `6 mm`, about a pencil eraser
- **E**volving: changing in size, shape, color, or starting to itch or bleed

Evolution is the single most important feature. The ugly duckling sign is also powerful: the mole that looks different from all of that person's other moles deserves attention regardless of ABCDE.

Breslow depth, measured in millimeters from the top of the granular layer to the deepest tumor cell, is the strongest prognostic factor. Thin melanomas under `1 mm` have `5`-year survival above `95%`; deeper lesions drop sharply. That is why suspicious pigmented lesions get excisional biopsy, not a shave.

> **Trap:** Melanoma is not only a fair-skin disease. In darker skin it more often appears on palms, soles, and under nails (acral lentiginous) and is caught later, which worsens outcomes. Examine palms, soles, and nails on everyone.

Dysplastic (atypical) nevi are larger than `5 mm` with irregular borders and uneven color. Most never become melanoma, but having many marks higher risk and warrants regular skin surveillance.

## Risk and prevention

Risk factors: fair skin (Fitzpatrick `I` and `II`), red or blond hair, more than `50` moles, blistering sunburns in childhood, tanning bed use, family or personal history of melanoma, immunosuppression, and chronic sun exposure.

Prevention: broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF `30` or higher applied `15` minutes before going out and reapplied every `2` hours or after swimming, shade between `10` a.m. and `4` p.m., protective clothing and wide-brimmed hats, and no tanning beds. Indoor tanning before age `35` raises melanoma risk by roughly `75%`.

> **On shift:** Any full-body skin exam should include scalp, between the toes, soles, nails, and behind the ears. Those are exactly where lesions hide until they are late.
keyPoints: Actinic keratosis is precancerous sandpaper-like roughness on sun-exposed skin.
Basal cell carcinoma: pearly rolled border, telangiectasias, rarely metastasizes, destroys locally.
Squamous cell carcinoma can metastasize, especially on lip and ear and in transplant patients.
Melanoma ABCDE with evolution as the strongest single feature; Breslow depth drives prognosis.
Examine palms, soles, and nails: acral melanoma is easy to miss in darker skin.

checks.q: A 70-year-old has a 7 mm pearly nodule on the nose with rolled edges, fine surface vessels, and a central crust that bleeds and recrusts for 8 months. Most likely:
checks.why: Pearly translucency, rolled borders, telangiectasias, and a non-healing central ulcer are hallmark basal cell carcinoma. Actinic keratosis is a rough flat patch, and seborrheic keratosis is a waxy stuck-on plaque without ulceration.

checks.q: Which single feature of a pigmented lesion is most concerning for melanoma?
choices: Change in size, shape, or color over recent months
checks.why: Evolution is the strongest ABCDE feature; a stable 6 mm uniformly pigmented mole is far less worrying than one that is changing. Sun exposure is a risk factor, not a lesion feature.

checks.q: Which prognostic factor matters most for a newly diagnosed melanoma?
checks.why: Breslow depth, the vertical thickness of tumor invasion, is the strongest predictor of survival and drives staging. Surface diameter and color variation help detection, not staging.

lessons.title: Wounds, pressure injuries, burns, and infant skin
lessons.body:
This is the skin content you use with your hands: wounds that need to close, skin that is dying under a patient, burns that need sizing, and babies whose rashes are mostly harmless except when they are not.

## How wounds heal

Four overlapping phases:

1. Hemostasis, within minutes: vessels constrict, platelets plug, fibrin clots.
2. Inflammation, days `1` to `4`: neutrophils then macrophages clear debris and bacteria. Redness and swelling here are normal, not infection.
3. Proliferation, days `4` to `21`: fibroblasts lay collagen, new vessels grow, the wound contracts and re-epithelializes.
4. Remodeling, `3` weeks to `1` year or more: collagen reorganizes. A healed scar tops out at about `80%` of original tensile strength.

Healing stalls with poor perfusion, diabetes, smoking, malnutrition (especially low protein and vitamin C), infection, steroids, and ongoing pressure.

## Closing a laceration

Irrigate with copious normal saline or clean tap water under pressure, roughly `50` to `100 mL` per centimeter of wound. Irrigation volume matters more than antiseptic. Explore for foreign bodies and check function of tendons, nerves, and vessels distal to the wound before anesthetizing.

Most wounds can be closed within `6` to `12` hours; clean facial wounds with good blood supply can often be closed up to `24` hours. Bites, heavily contaminated wounds, and puncture wounds are usually left open or loosely approximated.

Suture removal timing by site:

| Site | Days |
|---|---|
| Face | `3` to `5` |
| Scalp, neck | `7` |
| Arm, hand, trunk | `7` to `10` |
| Leg, foot | `10` to `14` |
| Over a joint | `10` to `14` |

Tetanus: if the last booster was over `10` years ago for a clean minor wound, or over `5` years for a dirty or puncture wound, update it.

> **Trap:** Never inject local anesthetic containing epinephrine and then assume you can leave a tourniquet-like effect in place. Modern practice does allow epinephrine in fingers and the nose, but check protocol before assuming.

## Pressure injuries

Sustained pressure over a bony prominence cuts off blood flow; tissue dies from the bone outward, so what you see on the surface understates the damage.

- Stage `1`: intact skin, non-blanching redness
- Stage `2`: partial-thickness loss, shallow open ulcer or intact serum-filled blister
- Stage `3`: full-thickness, fat visible, no bone/tendon/muscle exposed
- Stage `4`: full-thickness with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle
- Unstageable: base covered by slough or eschar, so depth cannot be seen
- Deep tissue injury: intact or blistered skin that is persistently deep purple or maroon

> **Key:** Prevention beats treatment: reposition at least every `2` hours in bed and every `1` hour in a chair, use pressure-redistributing surfaces, keep skin clean and dry, manage incontinence, and maintain nutrition. Never massage a reddened bony prominence.

## Burns

Superficial (first-degree) burns are red and painful with no blisters and heal in `3` to `6` days. Superficial partial-thickness burns blister, are wet and very painful, and heal in `1` to `3` weeks. Deep partial-thickness burns are drier, mottled, and less sensitive. Full-thickness (third-degree) burns are leathery white, brown, or charred, and painless in the burned area because nerve endings are destroyed.

Rule of nines in adults: head `9%`, each arm `9%`, each leg `18%`, front torso `18%`, back torso `18%`, genitals `1%`. Children have proportionally larger heads, so pediatric charts shift toward head `18%` and each leg `14%`. The patient's own palm including fingers is roughly `1%` for scattered burns.

## Infant and child rashes

Diaper dermatitis from irritation spares the deep folds, because urine and stool do not reach them. If the folds are involved with satellite pustules, it is candida and needs a topical antifungal. Frequent changes, barrier zinc oxide paste, and air time are the mainstays.

Erythema toxicum neonatorum: blotchy red macules with tiny central yellow-white papules appearing days `1` to `3`, involving up to half of newborns, harmless, gone within `2` weeks.

Milia: `1` to `2 mm` firm white keratin cysts on the nose and cheeks, resolving on their own; never squeeze them.

Congenital dermal melanocytosis (formerly Mongolian spot): blue-gray flat patches over the lower back and buttocks in darker-skinned infants, present from birth, fading over years. Document them clearly at birth so they are not later mistaken for bruising.

> **On shift:** A child with fever and a non-blanching rash is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise. Do the glass test, escalate immediately, and get blood cultures and IV antibiotics started within `1` hour. Waiting for the rash to spread is how children die.
keyPoints: Wound healing is hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodeling; scar reaches about 80% of original strength.
Suture removal: face 3 to 5 days, trunk and arms 7 to 10, legs and joints 10 to 14.
Pressure injury stages 1 to 4 plus unstageable and deep tissue injury; reposition every 2 hours.
Rule of nines: adult head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, torso 18% front and back; palm equals 1%.
Fever plus a non-blanching rash in a child means meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise.

checks.q: A sacral wound has full-thickness loss with visible subcutaneous fat but no exposed bone, tendon, or muscle. This is:
checks.why: Stage 3 is full-thickness with fat visible but no deeper structures exposed. Stage 2 is partial thickness, stage 4 exposes bone or tendon, and unstageable means slough or eschar blocks the view.

checks.q: An adult has circumferential burns to one entire arm and the entire anterior torso. Using the rule of nines, the approximate burned surface area is:
checks.why: One full arm is 9% and the anterior torso is 18%, totaling 27%. 18% alone ignores the arm and 36% would require an additional 9% region.

checks.q: An 18-month-old has a fever of 39.2 C and scattered dark red spots that do not fade under glass pressure. The correct action is:
choices: Treat immediately as meningococcal sepsis with blood cultures and IV antibiotics within 1 hour
checks.why: Fever with a non-blanching rash in a child is meningococcemia until excluded, and delay increases mortality steeply. Outpatient reassurance and symptomatic topical or oral therapy are unsafe here.

cards.front: Which skin layer has no blood vessels of its own, and what does that mean for healing?
cards.back: The epidermis. It feeds by diffusion from the dermis below, so damage confined to it heals without a scar.

cards.front: What is the size cutoff separating a macule from a patch, or a papule from a plaque?
cards.back: 1 cm. Macule and papule are under 1 cm; patch and plaque are over 1 cm.

cards.front: What is the difference between a vesicle and a bulla?
cards.back: Both are fluid-filled blisters. A vesicle is under 1 cm; a bulla is over 1 cm.

cards.front: What separates an erosion from an ulcer clinically?
cards.back: An erosion loses only epidermis and heals without a scar. An ulcer reaches the dermis or deeper and scars.

cards.front: A patient has leathery, thickened skin with exaggerated skin lines. What is it and what caused it?
cards.back: Lichenification, caused by months of chronic rubbing or scratching. It tells you the itch is long-standing.

cards.front: Give the size ranges for petechiae, purpura, and ecchymosis.
cards.back: Petechiae under 2 mm, purpura 2 mm to 1 cm, ecchymosis over 1 cm. All are non-blanching.

cards.front: What does it mean when a red lesion does not blanch under a glass slide?
cards.back: Blood has leaked out of the vessels into the tissue. Think platelet disorders, vasculitis, or meningococcal sepsis.

cards.front: Which rash favors flexural creases and which favors extensor surfaces?
cards.back: Atopic dermatitis favors flexural creases (inner elbows, behind knees). Psoriasis favors extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, shins).

cards.front: A vesicular rash forms a stripe on one side and stops sharply at the midline. What is it?
cards.back: Herpes zoster (shingles). A dermatomal distribution follows one sensory nerve root and does not cross the midline.

cards.front: What does an annular configuration with a scaly advancing edge and central clearing suggest?
cards.back: Tinea corporis (ringworm). The fungus grows outward, so the active scale is at the ring's edge.

cards.front: What is a target lesion, and which disease does it define?
cards.back: A three-zone lesion: dark or blistered center, pale ring, red outer ring. It defines erythema multiforme.

cards.front: What is koebnerization, and which three diseases classically show it?
cards.back: New lesions appearing along a scratch or scar. Seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo.

cards.front: What is a positive Nikolsky sign, and which three diagnoses does it raise?
cards.back: Lateral pressure on normal skin shears the epidermis off. Raises SJS/TEN, staph scalded skin syndrome, and pemphigus vulgaris.

cards.front: Why is excisional rather than shave biopsy preferred for a suspected melanoma?
cards.back: It preserves full thickness so Breslow depth can be measured. A shave can transect the tumor and make depth unmeasurable.

cards.front: A child has crusted erosions around the mouth with thick honey-colored crust. Diagnosis and first-line treatment?
cards.back: Non-bullous impetigo. Topical mupirocin 2% three times daily for 5 days if limited; oral cephalexin if widespread.

cards.front: What is the definitive treatment for a cutaneous abscess, and why are antibiotics not enough?
cards.back: Incision and drainage. Antibiotics do not penetrate a walled-off pocket of pus, so the pus must be released.

cards.front: Name four reasons to add oral antibiotics after draining an abscess.
cards.back: Surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs such as fever, immunosuppression or extremes of age, size over about 2 cm, or face and hand location.

cards.front: How do you tell erysipelas from cellulitis at the bedside?
cards.back: Erysipelas has a sharply demarcated raised border you can feel, is fire-engine red, and starts abruptly with fever. Cellulitis has indistinct fading borders.

cards.front: Which three oral antibiotics cover community MRSA?
cards.back: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, and clindamycin. Cephalexin does not cover MRSA and is used for non-purulent strep cellulitis.

cards.front: What is the single earliest and most reliable clue to necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.back: Pain far out of proportion to the visible skin findings, because nerves along the fascia are destroyed before the surface looks bad.

cards.front: What is the definitive treatment for necrotizing fasciitis, and what must not delay it?
cards.back: Immediate surgical debridement plus broad IV antibiotics and fluids. Imaging must not delay the operating room. Mortality runs roughly 20% to 30%.

cards.front: What skin finding tells you a virus from the herpes family is responsible?
cards.back: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. This applies to HSV, varicella, and zoster.

cards.front: What is the antiviral window for herpes zoster, and what does treatment achieve?
cards.back: Within 72 hours of rash onset. It shortens the acute episode and reduces the risk of postherpetic neuralgia.

cards.front: Vesicles appear on the tip of a patient's nose during shingles. What is that called and why does it matter?
cards.back: Hutchinson sign. The nasociliary branch is involved, predicting herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Needs same-day ophthalmology to prevent vision loss.

cards.front: A nurse has a painful fingertip with clustered vesicles. What is it and what must you not do?
cards.back: Herpetic whitlow. Do not incise and drain it; that spreads virus without helping. Treat with oral antivirals.

cards.front: What is eczema herpeticum and how is it treated?
cards.back: HSV spreading across eczematous skin as monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever. It is an emergency treated with systemic acyclovir.

cards.front: What are Koplik spots and when do they appear?
cards.back: Tiny white grains on red buccal mucosa, appearing 1 to 2 days before the measles rash. They are pathognomonic for measles.

cards.front: What are the three C's of measles, and what isolation is required?
cards.back: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, plus high fever. Measles is airborne, so mask and place in airborne isolation immediately.

cards.front: Which tinea infections require oral rather than topical antifungals, and why?
cards.back: Tinea capitis and tinea unguium. The fungus lives inside hair shafts and nail plate, which topical agents cannot penetrate.

cards.front: How does tinea cruris differ from candidal infection of the groin?
cards.back: Tinea cruris spares the scrotum and has a scaly advancing edge. Candida involves the scrotum and folds and shows satellite pustules.

cards.front: Where on a lesion should you scrape for a KOH prep, and what will you see?
cards.back: The advancing scaly edge. KOH dissolves human cells, leaving branching fungal hyphae, or spaghetti-and-meatballs in tinea versicolor.

cards.front: What is tinea incognito?
cards.back: A dermatophyte infection treated with topical steroids: redness and itch improve while the fungus spreads with a blurred, atypical border.

cards.front: Give the permethrin regimen for scabies.
cards.back: Permethrin 5% cream applied neck-down, left on 8 to 14 hours, repeated in 7 days. Infants also need scalp, face, palms, and soles.

cards.front: Why must all household contacts be treated for scabies at the same time?
cards.back: Itch takes 2 to 6 weeks to develop on first infestation, so contacts can be infested while asymptomatic and reinfest the treated patient.

cards.front: A patient still itches 3 weeks after correct scabies treatment. Is this failure?
cards.back: Usually no. Post-scabetic itch is an allergic reaction to residual mite antigen and lasts 2 to 4 weeks. New burrows, not itch alone, indicate failure.

cards.front: What is the atopic triad, and where does eczema appear in children versus infants?
cards.back: Atopic dermatitis, asthma, and allergic rhinitis. Infants get cheeks and outer arms; children and adults get flexural creases.

cards.front: How do you distinguish irritant from allergic contact dermatitis?
cards.back: Irritant burns, needs no prior sensitization, and appears within hours. Allergic itches, requires sensitization, and peaks 48 to 72 hours later.

cards.front: Name three nail findings of psoriasis.
cards.back: Pitting, oil-drop discoloration, and onycholysis (separation of the nail from its bed). Nail disease raises suspicion for psoriatic arthritis.

cards.front: What proportion of psoriasis patients develop psoriatic arthritis, and how does it present?
cards.back: About 30%. It favors distal finger joints and produces sausage-shaped digits (dactylitis).

cards.front: What are the six P's of lichen planus, and which infection is associated?
cards.back: Purple, polygonal, pruritic, planar papules with Wickham striae on wrists and ankles. Associated with hepatitis C.

cards.front: How do you recognize bradykinin-mediated angioedema, and why does it change treatment?
cards.back: Swelling with no hives and no itch, often on an ACE inhibitor. Antihistamines, steroids, and epinephrine are largely ineffective; protect the airway.

cards.front: Which topical steroid potency goes on the face and folds, and why?
cards.back: Low potency such as hydrocortisone 1% to 2.5% (class 7). Thin skin absorbs more and atrophies faster. Limit potent steroids to about 2 weeks continuously.

cards.front: What four features turn a simple drug rash into a dermatologic emergency?
cards.back: Mucous membrane involvement, blisters or skin detachment, skin pain, and fever. Any of these means stop the drug and escalate.

cards.front: Give the body surface area cutoffs for SJS, overlap, and TEN.
cards.back: SJS under 10% detachment, SJS/TEN overlap 10% to 30%, TEN over 30%. Mortality is roughly 5% for SJS and 30% or more for TEN.

cards.front: Name five drugs most associated with SJS/TEN.
cards.back: Allopurinol, sulfonamides, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, and phenytoin. Nevirapine and oxicam NSAIDs also carry high risk.

cards.front: What is the timing and lab signature of DRESS?
cards.back: Onset 2 to 8 weeks after the drug, with fever, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia often above 700 cells per microliter, and hepatitis.

cards.front: What is the epinephrine dose and route for anaphylaxis in an adult and a small child?
cards.back: 0.3 mg IM into the outer thigh for adults, 0.15 mg for children under 30 kg, repeatable every 5 to 15 minutes.

cards.front: What single finding separates staph scalded skin syndrome from TEN?
cards.back: Mucous membranes are spared in SSSS. TEN requires erosions at two or more mucosal sites. SSSS is toxin-mediated in children under 5.

cards.front: A febrile patient has rapidly spreading non-blanching purpura and hypotension. What is the action?
cards.back: Treat as meningococcemia or purpura fulminans: blood cultures and IV antibiotics ideally within 1 hour, plus aggressive fluid resuscitation.

cards.front: What are the four steps in acne pathogenesis?
cards.back: Follicular plugging with keratin, excess sebum under androgen drive, Cutibacterium acnes overgrowth, and inflammation.

cards.front: Why is a topical retinoid first-line for comedonal acne?
cards.back: Retinoids normalize keratin shedding, so they are the only agents that both treat existing comedones and prevent new ones.

cards.front: Why is a topical antibiotic for acne never used alone?
cards.back: It breeds Cutibacterium acnes resistance. Pair it with benzoyl peroxide, which kills bacteria without generating resistance.

cards.front: What are the isotretinoin dosing targets and the mandatory monitoring program?
cards.back: About 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day to a cumulative 120 to 150 mg/kg. Requires iPLEDGE enrollment, two contraceptive methods, monthly pregnancy tests, plus lipid and liver monitoring.

cards.front: Which single finding rules out rosacea and points to acne instead?
cards.back: Comedones. Rosacea never produces blackheads or whiteheads. Topical steroids worsen rosacea.

cards.front: How does alopecia areata look, and what conditions travel with it?
cards.back: Sudden smooth round bald patches without scale or scarring, sometimes with exclamation-point hairs and nail pitting. Associated with thyroid disease and vitiligo.

cards.front: What is the timeline of telogen effluvium?
cards.back: Diffuse shedding starting 2 to 3 months after a stressor such as childbirth, surgery, or illness, resolving in 6 to 9 months once the trigger is gone.

cards.front: What is an actinic keratosis and how fast does it become cancer?
cards.back: A rough sandpaper-like precancerous patch on sun-exposed skin. Roughly 0.1% to 1% per lesion per year progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.front: Describe the classic appearance and behavior of basal cell carcinoma.
cards.back: Pearly translucent papule with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and a central ulcer that bleeds and recrusts. It metastasizes under 0.1% but destroys locally.

cards.front: Which sites make a squamous cell carcinoma higher risk for metastasis?
cards.back: Lip and ear especially, plus any lesion in a transplant patient on immunosuppression, whose risk is 65 to 100 times the general population.

cards.front: Spell out the ABCDE rule and name the most important letter.
cards.back: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolving. Evolution is the strongest single feature.

cards.front: What is Breslow depth and why does it dominate melanoma prognosis?
cards.back: Vertical tumor thickness in millimeters from the granular layer to the deepest tumor cell. Lesions under 1 mm have 5-year survival above 95%.

cards.front: Where does melanoma tend to appear in patients with darker skin?
cards.back: Palms, soles, and under the nails (acral lentiginous melanoma). It is often found later, so examine those sites on everyone.

cards.front: Give the practical sunscreen rules.
cards.back: Broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, applied 15 minutes before exposure, reapplied every 2 hours or after swimming or sweating. Seek shade from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

cards.front: Name the four phases of wound healing with their timing.
cards.back: Hemostasis within minutes, inflammation days 1 to 4, proliferation days 4 to 21, remodeling from 3 weeks to over a year.

cards.front: Give suture removal timing for face, trunk, and lower leg.
cards.back: Face 3 to 5 days, scalp and neck about 7, arm/hand/trunk 7 to 10, leg/foot and joints 10 to 14 days.

cards.front: Distinguish pressure injury stage 2 from stage 3.
cards.back: Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss, a shallow ulcer or intact serum blister. Stage 3 is full-thickness with visible fat but no exposed bone, tendon, or muscle.

cards.front: Give the repositioning intervals for pressure injury prevention.
cards.back: At least every 2 hours in bed and every 1 hour in a chair, plus pressure-redistributing surfaces, dry skin, and good nutrition. Never massage a reddened bony prominence.

cards.front: Give the adult rule of nines percentages.
cards.back: Head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior torso 18%, posterior torso 18%, genitals 1%. The patient's palm with fingers is about 1%.

cards.front: How do you tell irritant diaper dermatitis from candidal diaper rash?
cards.back: Irritant dermatitis spares the deep folds because urine and stool do not reach them. Candida involves the folds and has satellite pustules.

cards.front: What is erythema toxicum neonatorum?
cards.back: Blotchy red macules with tiny central yellow-white papules appearing on days 1 to 3, affecting up to half of newborns. It is benign and clears within 2 weeks.

quiz.q: A flat, non-palpable area of color change measuring 3 cm is best described as which primary lesion?
quiz.why: Flat plus over 1 cm equals a patch. A macule is flat but under 1 cm, and plaque and nodule are both palpable and raised.

quiz.q: Which pair of findings tells you a lesion is non-blanching?
choices: It fades completely under a glass slide and is warm
It is raised and resolves within 24 hours
It has silvery scale that flakes off
It does not fade under a glass slide because blood is outside the vessels
quiz.why: Diascopy separates dilated vessels, which blanch, from extravasated blood, which does not. Wheals blanch and resolve in under 24 hours; silvery scale describes psoriasis.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old has pinpoint dark red spots 1 to 2 mm across on the lower legs that do not blanch. These are:
quiz.why: Non-blanching lesions under 2 mm are petechiae. Wheals blanch, papules are solid raised bumps, and vesicles contain clear fluid.

quiz.q: A clinician documents 'annular plaques with a raised scaly advancing border and central clearing on the trunk.' Before any test, the most likely diagnosis is:
quiz.why: Ring shape with an actively scaling edge and clear center is dermatophyte growth outward, so tinea corporis. Psoriasis plaques are solid with silvery scale, zoster is dermatomal and vesicular, and EM makes three-zone targets.

quiz.q: A patient with psoriasis develops a new linear plaque exactly along a recent scratch. This phenomenon is called:
quiz.why: Koebnerization is new disease appearing at sites of trauma, seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo. Auspitz is pinpoint bleeding under scale, Nikolsky is epidermal shearing, Hutchinson relates to zoster of the nose tip or nail pigment.

quiz.q: Firm lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin adjacent to a blister causes the epidermis to slide off. Which diagnosis is LEAST consistent with this finding?
quiz.why: A positive Nikolsky sign means the epidermis is detaching, seen in TEN, SSSS, and pemphigus. Tinea versicolor is a superficial yeast causing fine scaly patches with no epidermal separation.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old has crusted erosions with thick honey-colored crust around the nose, limited to a 3 cm area. Best initial therapy is:
choices: Topical mupirocin 2% three times daily for 5 days
quiz.why: Limited non-bullous impetigo responds to topical mupirocin. Steroids worsen infection, there is no abscess to drain, and acyclovir treats herpes, not staph or strep.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old has a rapidly spreading leg infection with pain far out of proportion to appearance, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, and a blood pressure of 86/48. The single most important intervention is:
choices: Immediate surgical consultation for operative debridement
CT scan before any other step
quiz.why: These are necrotizing fasciitis findings, and survival depends on emergent debridement. Imaging must not delay the operating room, and oral antibiotics or conservative measures are grossly inadequate.

quiz.q: Which antibiotic choice does NOT provide reliable coverage for community-acquired MRSA?
quiz.why: Cephalexin covers streptococci and methicillin-sensitive staph but not MRSA. TMP-SMX, doxycycline, and clindamycin are the standard oral MRSA options.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old has bilateral lower-leg redness, scaling, itching, chronic swelling, and no fever. The most likely diagnosis is:
quiz.why: Bilateral, itchy, afebrile leg redness with chronic edema is stasis dermatitis from venous insufficiency. Cellulitis and erysipelas are nearly always unilateral, painful, and often febrile.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old presents 36 hours after the onset of a painful vesicular rash in one thoracic dermatome. What is the best action?
choices: Withhold antivirals because the rash already appeared
quiz.why: The 72-hour window from rash onset is still open, and antivirals reduce acute pain and postherpetic neuralgia. Antibacterials do not treat a viral eruption and steroids alone are not the answer.

quiz.q: A patient with shingles on the forehead has vesicles at the tip of the nose. This finding requires:
choices: Incision and drainage of the vesicles
quiz.why: Vesicles on the nasal tip (Hutchinson sign) indicate nasociliary involvement and predict herpes zoster ophthalmicus, which can cause vision loss. Delay risks permanent damage.

quiz.q: Which combination of findings is most specific for measles?
choices: Slapped-cheek redness with a lacy arm rash
Three days of high fever then a trunk rash after defervescence
Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and white grains on the buccal mucosa
Oral ulcers with oval vesicles on palms and soles
quiz.why: The three C's plus Koplik spots define measles. Slapped cheeks are fifth disease, fever-then-rash is roseola, and oral ulcers with acral vesicles are hand-foot-and-mouth disease.

quiz.q: Dome-shaped pearly papules with a central dimple in a 6-year-old are most consistent with:
quiz.why: Central umbilication is the signature of molluscum contagiosum. Warts are rough with black dots, varicella lesions are vesicular in multiple stages, and impetigo forms honey-colored crust.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old has scaly scalp patches with black-dot broken hairs and tender cervical nodes. Which statement is correct?
choices: Oral antifungal therapy for several weeks is required
quiz.why: Tinea capitis involves the hair shaft, so systemic therapy such as griseofulvin or terbinafine is required. Topicals cannot penetrate the shaft and steroids worsen fungal infection.

quiz.q: A KOH preparation of scale shows branching hyphae. This confirms:
quiz.why: KOH dissolves keratinocytes and leaves fungal cell walls, so visible hyphae confirm a dermatophyte. Scabies is confirmed by mites or eggs on scraping, and neither cellulitis nor contact dermatitis has hyphae.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old with obesity has a beefy-red, sharply bordered plaque beneath the pannus with small pustules just outside the plaque. Best treatment is:
choices: Topical clotrimazole plus keeping the fold dry
quiz.why: Satellite pustules in a moist fold indicate candidal intertrigo, treated with a topical azole and moisture control. Terbinafine targets dermatophytes, permethrin treats scabies, and potent steroids worsen yeast.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has dry, intensely itchy plaques in both antecubital fossae with excoriations, plus a history of asthma. The single most important long-term measure is:
choices: Consistent emollient use and barrier repair
quiz.why: Atopic dermatitis is a barrier defect, so emollients are the backbone of control and reduce steroid need. Chronic potent steroids cause atrophy, and antibiotics and antifungals do not treat the underlying disease.

quiz.q: A patient has well-demarcated salmon plaques with silvery scale on both elbows and knees, nail pitting, and morning stiffness in the distal finger joints. What complication is developing?
