quiz.why: Psoriasis plus nail pitting plus distal interphalangeal involvement points to psoriatic arthritis, which occurs in about 30% of psoriasis patients. Gout is acute and monoarticular, and septic arthritis is febrile and rapidly destructive.

quiz.q: A 25-year-old has a single large scaly oval on the trunk, followed 10 days later by many smaller ovals oriented along skin lines. What must be excluded before reassuring the patient?
choices: Secondary syphilis, especially if palms and soles are involved
quiz.why: Pityriasis rosea is self-limited, but secondary syphilis mimics it and characteristically involves palms and soles, so serology is warranted when those sites are affected.

quiz.q: A patient taking lamotrigine for 2 weeks develops painful skin, dusky macules, oral and conjunctival erosions, and epidermal detachment over 8% of body surface area. The diagnosis is:
quiz.why: Detachment under 10% of BSA with two-site mucosal involvement defines SJS. TEN requires over 30%, DRESS features eosinophilia and hepatitis without detachment, and EM minor spares mucosa.

quiz.q: What is the single most important first action for any suspected severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction?
quiz.why: Stopping the culprit drug limits ongoing injury and improves survival, and it precedes all other steps. Steroids are controversial, biopsy does not change immediate action, and prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended.

quiz.q: A patient started carbamazepine 6 weeks ago and now has facial swelling, a widespread rash, temperature 39 C, eosinophils 2,100/microliter, and transaminases four times normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
quiz.why: Delayed onset with fever, facial edema, eosinophilia, and hepatitis is DRESS. EM shows target lesions without organ injury, anaphylaxis is minutes-fast, and a fixed drug eruption is a few localized recurring plaques.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old has fever, diffuse tender erythema with superficial peeling, a positive Nikolsky sign, and completely normal mouth and eyes. Best treatment is:
quiz.why: Mucosal sparing with peeling in a young child is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, driven by a staph exfoliative toxin, so anti-staphylococcal antibiotics are required. Mucosal involvement would suggest SJS/TEN instead.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old develops hives, throat tightness, and wheezing 10 minutes after eating shrimp. Which action must occur first?
choices: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM into the outer thigh
quiz.why: IM epinephrine is the only treatment that reverses anaphylaxis and must never be delayed. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, and observation alone risks airway collapse.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old has numerous blackheads and whiteheads with a few papules and no nodules. The best initial regimen is:
quiz.why: A retinoid addresses the keratin plug and benzoyl peroxide covers the inflammatory component without promoting resistance. Isotretinoin is reserved for severe scarring acne and clindamycin alone breeds resistance.

quiz.q: Which requirement applies to a patient of childbearing potential starting isotretinoin?
choices: iPLEDGE enrollment, two contraceptive methods, and monthly pregnancy tests
quiz.why: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen, so the iPLEDGE program mandates dual contraception and monthly pregnancy testing, with lipid and liver enzyme monitoring. Ultrasound and blood pressure logs are not part of the program.

quiz.q: A 48-year-old has central facial erythema, telangiectasias, and pustules with no comedones, worsened by heat and alcohol. Which treatment is contraindicated?
quiz.why: Potent topical steroids worsen rosacea and can cause steroid-induced rosacea with rebound. Metronidazole, ivermectin, and doxycycline are all accepted rosacea therapies.

quiz.q: A 32-year-old has recurrent painful nodules, draining sinus tracts, and rope-like scars in both axillae and the groin. The diagnosis is:
quiz.why: Recurrent nodules with sinus tracts and scarring in apocrine-bearing folds is hidradenitis suppurativa, a follicular occlusion disease linked to smoking and obesity, not hygiene. Scabies causes burrows and itch, not sinus tracts.

quiz.q: Which pigmented-lesion feature carries the greatest weight in deciding to biopsy?
choices: Recent change in size, color, or shape
quiz.why: Evolution is the most predictive ABCDE criterion. A small, symmetric, stable lesion is reassuring regardless of location, and body site alone does not drive the decision.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old farmer has a firm, tender, crusted nodule on the lower lip that has enlarged over 4 months. The greatest concern is:
choices: Basal cell carcinoma with negligible metastatic risk
Squamous cell carcinoma, which on the lip carries meaningful metastatic risk
quiz.why: Lip lesions that are firm, tender, and enlarging suggest squamous cell carcinoma, where lip and ear sites carry higher metastatic potential. Basal cell rarely metastasizes, and an actinic keratosis would be flat and rough, not nodular.

quiz.q: A 41-year-old with deeply pigmented skin has an irregular dark patch on the sole that has widened over a year. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Melanoma is unlikely because of skin tone
Acral lentiginous melanoma must be excluded with biopsy
quiz.why: Melanoma in darker skin most often appears on palms, soles, and nail beds and is diagnosed later, worsening outcomes. An enlarging irregular acral pigmented lesion warrants biopsy, not reassurance.

quiz.q: A facial laceration is repaired with simple interrupted sutures. Removal should occur at approximately:
quiz.why: Facial wounds heal quickly with excellent blood supply, and early removal minimizes suture track marks. Longer intervals apply to trunk, extremities, and joints.

quiz.q: A bedbound patient has a heel wound whose base is covered entirely with thick black eschar. This is classified as:
quiz.why: When eschar or slough hides the wound base, depth cannot be determined, so it is unstageable until debrided. Deep tissue injury describes intact or blistered skin that is persistently purple or maroon.

quiz.q: An adult has burns to the entire posterior torso and the entire right leg. Estimated burned body surface area is:
quiz.why: Posterior torso is 18% and one full leg is 18%, giving 36%. Choosing 27% would substitute an arm for the leg, and 18% counts only one region.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old has a temperature of 39.4 C, appears lethargic, and has spreading dark red spots that do not blanch. The correct action is:
choices: Apply a topical steroid and reassess in the morning
Obtain blood cultures and give IV antibiotics within 1 hour while resuscitating
quiz.why: Fever with a non-blanching rash in a child is meningococcal sepsis until excluded, and each hour of antibiotic delay increases mortality. Outpatient or topical management is unsafe.

quiz.q: Which statement about wound healing is correct?
choices: Redness and swelling on day 2 always indicate infection
Remodeling is complete within one week
A mature scar regains about 80% of original tensile strength
quiz.why: Scar tissue tops out near 80% of original strength after months of remodeling. Early redness and swelling are the normal inflammatory phase, remodeling lasts up to a year or more, and hemostasis comes first.

scenarios.title: Triage: 58-year-old with a red, painful leg
scenarios.intro: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes walks into the emergency department at 2140 with his wife. She says the redness on his right calf started yesterday morning and has "taken over the whole leg" since dinner. He is pale, sweating, and cannot stay still in the chair. You are the tech rooming him.

steps.prompt: He is in the triage chair. The right calf is red and swollen. He rates the pain a `10` and says even the air hurts. What do you do first?

choices.text: Take a full set of vitals, get him into a room immediately, and tell the charge nurse the pain is far out of proportion to what the leg looks like
choices.feedback: Correct. Tachycardia, hypotension, fever, and pain out of proportion together are a necrotizing infection pattern. Speed matters more than a perfect history here.

choices.text: Put him in the waiting room and recheck in 30 minutes
choices.feedback: Harmful. A heart rate of 124 with a systolic of 98 and fever is early septic shock. Thirty minutes of waiting is 30 minutes of fascia dying.

choices.text: Get vitals but wait to tell anyone until the full triage note is typed
choices.feedback: Acceptable but slow. Documentation can follow the verbal report. Say the words out loud first.

choices.text: Apply a warm compress and elevate the leg before taking vitals
choices.feedback: Harmful. Comfort measures before recognizing shock delays the only thing that helps, which is antibiotics and a surgeon.

steps.prompt: He is in a resuscitation room. The PA asks you to help expose and examine the leg. The redness is dusky purple in the center, there is a `4 cm` blood-filled blister, and when you press near the knee you feel a faint crackling under the skin.

choices.text: Report the crepitus and the hemorrhagic bulla to the PA immediately and mark the edge of the redness with a pen and the time
choices.feedback: Correct. Crepitus means gas-forming organisms in tissue, and a hemorrhagic bulla means tissue death. Marking the border makes spread over the next 20 minutes objective and visible.

choices.text: Unroof the blister to see what is under it
choices.feedback: Harmful. Opening it adds a portal for infection and gives you nothing management does not already know from the outside.

choices.text: Note the findings and mention them when the PA finishes the abdominal exam
choices.feedback: Too slow. Crepitus changes the plan from admission to operating room. Interrupt.

choices.text: Photograph the leg for the chart before saying anything
choices.feedback: Acceptable in principle, wrong in sequence. Documentation never precedes communication in a time-critical finding.

steps.prompt: The PA suspects necrotizing fasciitis. Labs are drawn: white count `21,000`, sodium `128`, C-reactive protein `240`, creatinine `1.9`, glucose `242`. The attending is calling surgery. You are asked what should happen next.

choices.text: Two large-bore IVs, fluid resuscitation, blood cultures, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics now, with surgery mobilizing for the operating room
choices.feedback: Correct. Antibiotics and fluids buy time; only debridement is definitive. Cultures are drawn before antibiotics when it does not delay them.

choices.text: Send him to CT first and hold antibiotics until the scan resolves the diagnosis
choices.feedback: Harmful. Imaging is supportive at best and a normal scan does not rule this out. Nothing should delay antibiotics or the operating room.

choices.text: Calculate the LRINEC score and let the number decide whether to call surgery
choices.feedback: Dangerous reliance on a score. LRINEC supports suspicion but a low score never excludes necrotizing fasciitis. Clinical findings win.

choices.text: Start IV fluids and antibiotics while someone else arranges surgical consult
choices.feedback: Good. Parallel action is the right instinct. The only addition is drawing cultures before the first antibiotic dose if it costs no time.

steps.prompt: Surgery arrives within `12` minutes and takes him to the operating room. The wife asks you why nobody just gave him antibiotics and sent him home like last time he had a leg infection. How do you frame the answer?

choices.text: Explain plainly that this infection travels along the tissue layer under the skin faster than antibiotics can reach it, so surgery has to remove the dead tissue
choices.feedback: Correct. Plain mechanism, no jargon, no numbers thrown at a frightened family member. This is the right altitude.

choices.text: Tell her his LRINEC score was elevated and his SIRS criteria were met
choices.feedback: Unhelpful. Scores and acronyms mean nothing to her and sound evasive. Translate.

choices.text: Say you are not allowed to discuss anything and walk away
choices.feedback: Harmful to trust. You can explain the general situation and route specific questions to the PA or surgeon without shutting her out.

choices.text: Tell her it is probably just a bad cellulitis and he will be fine
choices.feedback: Harmful. False reassurance about a condition with roughly 20% to 30% mortality is both wrong and unkind when the truth arrives.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: pain out of proportion plus systemic toxicity equals necrotizing infection until a surgeon says otherwise. Every supporting finding here, dusky skin, hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, sodium of `128`, came after the pain did. That is the point. The earliest sign is the one the patient tells you, not the one you see. Antibiotics and fluids are a bridge; debridement is the treatment, and every hour of delay raises mortality. Marking the border with a pen and a time is a cheap, powerful way to turn "it looks worse" into documented fact.

scenarios.title: Working through a new rash step by step
scenarios.intro: You are given a case with no diagnosis attached and asked to reason out loud. A 29-year-old woman has a rash that started `6` days ago. She has no fever and feels well. Your job is to build the description before you build the diagnosis.

steps.prompt: You are told only that she "has a rash on her arms." What is the first thing you should establish?

choices.text: The primary lesion: flat or raised, solid or fluid-filled, and its size
choices.feedback: Correct. Every dermatologic reasoning chain starts with the primary lesion. Everything else narrows within that category.

choices.text: Which over-the-counter creams she already tried
choices.feedback: Useful later, and it can distort the picture through tinea incognito or steroid effect, but it is not step one.

choices.text: Whether she wants a steroid prescription
choices.feedback: Harmful sequencing. Choosing a treatment before characterizing the lesion is how tinea gets steroids and spreads.

choices.text: Her family history of skin cancer
choices.feedback: Relevant to a pigmented-lesion evaluation, not to characterizing an acute inflammatory rash.

steps.prompt: On exam: raised, solid, flat-topped papules `3` to `5 mm` across, violet in color, with fine white lace-like lines across their surface. They itch considerably. What have you established so far?

choices.text: Pruritic violaceous flat-topped papules with Wickham striae, which is a specific pattern
choices.feedback: Correct. You have named lesion, color, size, and surface. That combination is already narrow, and the white lines are a named finding.

choices.text: Vesicles, therefore a herpes family virus
choices.feedback: Incorrect. These are solid papules, not fluid-filled. Getting the primary lesion wrong sends the whole chain the wrong way.

choices.text: A plaque disease, therefore psoriasis
choices.feedback: Incorrect. These are discrete papules under 1 cm, not confluent plaques with silvery scale on extensors.

choices.text: An itchy papular rash, which could be many things pending distribution
choices.feedback: Safe but under-reading. You have more information than that: the color and the surface lines are diagnostic clues you skipped.

steps.prompt: Distribution: symmetric on the flexor wrists and both ankles. She also has lacy white patches on the inner cheeks. Where does this land?

choices.text: Lichen planus, remembered as purple, polygonal, pruritic, planar papules with Wickham striae and oral involvement
choices.feedback: Correct. Flexor wrists and ankles plus oral lacy patches completes the picture. The six P's are a memory device for exactly this presentation.

choices.text: Atopic dermatitis, because the wrists are involved
choices.feedback: Incorrect. Atopic dermatitis is dry, ill-defined, and flexural at the elbows and knees, and it does not produce violaceous flat-topped papules or oral lacy patches.

choices.text: Contact dermatitis from a bracelet
choices.feedback: Reasonable to consider with wrist involvement, but nickel dermatitis takes the shape of the object and would not explain bilateral ankles and oral lesions.

choices.text: Scabies, since it itches badly
choices.feedback: Itch alone is not enough. Scabies makes burrows in finger webs and waistline, not violaceous flat-topped papules with oral changes.

steps.prompt: You are asked what testing, if any, is warranted beyond the skin itself.

choices.text: Check hepatitis C serology, given the recognized association with lichen planus
choices.feedback: Correct. Lichen planus carries an association with hepatitis C, and identifying it changes management well beyond the skin.

choices.text: No testing at all; treat topically and move on
choices.feedback: Incomplete. Topical steroids are reasonable therapy, but skipping the hepatitis C consideration misses the systemic link.

choices.text: Order a KOH prep of the oral lesions
choices.feedback: KOH would address thrush, which scrapes off leaving a raw base. Lichen planus oral patches are lacy and fixed, so this does not fit.

choices.text: Order a full-body CT scan to search for malignancy
choices.feedback: Harmful overtesting. Nothing in this presentation suggests occult malignancy, and the scan carries cost and radiation for no gain.

steps.prompt: Final step: state the reasoning method you used, so it transfers to the next undiagnosed rash you see.

choices.text: Primary lesion first, then color and surface, then configuration and distribution, then associated sites and systemic links
choices.feedback: Correct. That order is reproducible and works whether the answer is common or rare. It also produces a usable note.

choices.text: Match the rash to the closest photo you remember and go with it
choices.feedback: This is pattern recognition without a safety net. It works until it doesn't, and it fails hardest on the dangerous rashes that mimic benign ones.

choices.text: Start with the treatment most likely to work and adjust from the response
choices.feedback: Harmful. Empiric steroids on an unrecognized fungal or infectious rash make it worse and obscure the diagnosis.

choices.text: Ask the patient what she thinks it is and treat accordingly
choices.feedback: Her history matters, but her self-diagnosis is not a substitute for morphologic reasoning.

scenarios.debrief: The method is the lesson. Name the primary lesion, then color and surface, then configuration and distribution, then look for associated mucosal or systemic findings. Here that chain ran: solid flat-topped papule, violet with white lace lines, symmetric on flexor wrists and ankles, plus lacy oral patches, which equals lichen planus and prompts hepatitis C testing. Notice that two of the wrong answers came from misnaming the primary lesion at step two. If the first link is wrong, every link after it is wrong, which is why morphology always precedes diagnosis.
